entry.evidence: The main purpose of this paper is to document these in-water explosions as they provide examples of low-magnitude events of interest to the CTBTO.

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text) with published PDF for figures

steps.action: The authors set two aims: use announced controlled explosions with known location and charge to assess IDC location accuracy and magnitudes, and extend in-water yield-magnitude relations to low magnitudes.
steps.quote: [...] to complement the few yield-magnitude relationships for in-water explosions available in the literature

steps.action: The authors take from the literature the expectation that in-water explosions couple better to the ground than underground explosions and so produce larger magnitudes for the same yield.
steps.quote: in-water explosions couple better to the surrounding media than underground explosions, triggering events of larger magnitudes for the same yield

steps.action: The authors used press reports quoting maritime authorities, and earlier conference posters, to identify controlled WW2 ordnance explosions with known time, position and charge in five areas (Gdansk, Swinoujscie, Brest, Skagen, Danube).
steps.quote: Three areas were identified where WW2 ordnances were destroyed in 2020

steps.action: The authors searched the REB, SEL3 and VSEL3 bulletins for events in these areas and matched further REB events to press reports, which gave nine REB events in the Gulf of Gdansk, three with a known explosion place.
steps.quote: These five areas were examined to check whether the REB contained any additional past events.

steps.action: The authors reviewed IDC locations (free depth where possible, all at 0 km) and IDC local magnitudes ML measured on a 2-4 Hz incoherent beam for each event.
steps.quote: Free depth solution was preferable if depth uncertainty was not too large.

steps.action: The authors compared automatic (SEL3, VSEL3) and reviewed (REB) locations with ground-truth positions: automatic solutions were poorly located, while REB locations lay within 20 km and their 90% ellipses contained the ground truth.
steps.quote: All events were located at less than 20 km from the place given by the authorities.

steps.action: The authors noted that Gulf of Gdansk explosions were recorded at Scandinavian stations but not at the GERES array, which lies at a similar distance.
steps.quote: Intuitively the explosions in the Gulf of Gdansk should have been detected at GERES, which was not the case.

steps.action: The authors adopted the published explanation that a low-velocity zone below the Tornquist-Teisseyre Zone blocks and scatters regional P energy on the path to GERES.
steps.quote: Schweitzer et al. proposed a model of low velocity zone below the TTZ which could explain blockage of seismic energy along the TTZ.

steps.action: The authors described the 5-ton Swinoujscie event: GA formed no SEL3 solution, NET-VISA listed it, analysts combined seven stations including GERES for the REB, and the first arrival automatically picked at GERES was Pg.
steps.quote: it was possible to combine observations from seven stations (VRAC, GERES, HFS, NOA, FINES, EKA and ARCES) to include this event in the REB

steps.action: The authors proposed two rival explanations for the different detection pattern (different propagation conditions at the site, or larger charge) and favoured charge size, without a test.
steps.quote: However, the main reason is more likely related to the larger size of the explosion.

steps.action: The authors examined explosions missing from the REB: Brest (two stations), two Skagen events (four stations, below threshold), and the Danube event, which they found on closer examination at GERES and the infrasound station I26DE.
steps.quote: upon closer examination, recordings were found of this event on the primary seismic array GERES

steps.action: The authors detected the Danube infrasound signal with PMCC (reprocessed offline) and located the event from GERES and I26DE readings.
steps.quote: IDC location based on readings from GERES and I26DE was 7 km from the reported explosion location

steps.action: The authors compared IDC locations of the non-REB events with ground truth: Brest was more than 50 km off, Skagen up to 24 km, and the Danube 7 km.
steps.quote: From eight investigated examples, location calculated at the IDC was at the largest distance from the ground truth

steps.action: The authors checked the IDC location errors against reference locations from denser networks (ISC bulletin for Brest; Larsen et al. for Skagen) and attributed the error to the sparse IMS network.
steps.quote: Additional local and regional network enabled to locate this event at the distance of 6 km from the source

steps.action: The authors compiled published yields and magnitudes of other in-water explosions (CHASE, Dead Sea 1999, Florida 2016) and IDC mb values for Florida 2021 (Table 3), together with the WW2 events.
steps.quote: Other examples of in-water explosions for which seismic magnitudes exist are also included in the graph

steps.action: The authors drew the published Murphy (1981) underground relation and the Gitterman and Shapira (2001) Dead Sea relation as expectations on the magnitude-yield graph.
steps.quote: (1) the standard Murphy (20) line; (2) the line derived by Gitterman and Shapira (7) for the 1999 Dead Sea experiments

steps.action: The authors compared all in-water points with the curves: every point falls well below the Murphy line, and the WW2 events sit at the low end of the yield range.
steps.quote: It is clear that all points fall well below the Murphy (20) curve.

steps.action: The authors proposed a 'modified Murphy' relation: the Murphy slope with one magnitude unit added to the constant, judged by eye to be a reasonable fit.
steps.quote: We propose this new magnitude-yield relationship for in-water explosions.

steps.action: The authors set aside the Gitterman relation as fitting worse and as specific to the dense, saline water of the Dead Sea.
steps.quote: it does account better than the Gitterman (2001) relationship, which has a different slope

steps.action: The authors kept the claim that the IMS network detects and locates 1-5 t in-water explosions, with REB locations within 20 km of ground truth and inside the 90% ellipses.
steps.quote: The distance between the IDC location and the source position was below 20 km.

steps.action: The authors kept the claim that an in-water explosion yields seismic amplitudes equal to those of an in-ground explosion with 17.2 times the yield.
steps.quote: from an in-ground explosion with 17.2 times the yield in kT

end.claim: In-water explosions produce seismic magnitudes about one unit higher than in-ground explosions of the same yield (equivalent to 17.2 times the yield), a relation extended here to the low-magnitude range (ML about 1.8-3.0).

decisive_move.sentence: Identifying announced controlled detonations with publicly reported position and charge supplied the ground truth without which neither the location-accuracy nor the yield-magnitude claim could be made.

gates.evidence: Data were routine IMS monitoring recordings, selected afterwards from press reports, with no hypothesis guiding acquisition. Location accuracy was tested against ground truth and could have failed: Brest, a non-REB event, was more than 50 km off. The modified-Murphy line was chosen by eye, with no goodness-of-fit test and acknowledged outliers (§6 ¶5). Nothing was fixed in advance.

imports.item: Press reports of time, position and charge of controlled detonations used as ground truth
Ground-truth information for 2012 Danish detonations, via Larsen et al.

novelty_claims.quote: This paper complements the literature of observations on the lower range of magnitudes.
We propose this new magnitude-yield relationship for in-water explosions.

limits: Sub-claims and their statuses: (1) REB events from 1-5 t charges are located within 20 km of ground truth, with ground truth inside the 90% ellipses: capability_characterized, from four events. (2) Events below 1 t were not in the bulletins but could be located within 50 km: capability_characterized. (3) The GERES non-detection of Gulf of Gdansk events is explained by TTZ blockage: best_explanation, cited from Schweitzer 1995, not tested here. (4) The Swinoujscie detection pattern is due to charge size rather than site: an untested hypothesis. (5) Station combinations depend on crustal structure (§7 ¶2): asserted, not tested. Process limits: the modified-Murphy line is a by-eye static offset, with no fit, residuals or uncertainty reported. The 17.2 factor is not derived in the text; by inference it equals 10^(1/0.81) from the Murphy slope. Yields come from press reports and are not independently verified. The magnitude types are mixed (IDC ML, ISC ML, local ML, ISC mb, IDC mb) on one graph. Coupling parameters (water depth, seabed) are acknowledged as unknown (§6 ¶3), and the suggested simulations are not done (§6 ¶6). Inconsistencies: Table 1 gives 0.00500 kT for Swinoujscie while the Fig. 6 label gives 0.005400 kT; the text gives Gdansk ML 2.3-2.4 while Table 1 gives 2.4 for all three events. The abstract says the data are from 2020, but the 2012 events are included. Sample size is small (eight events), and how events were selected from press searches is not described in detail. No review file was supplied, so the review history is unknown.

disagreements.support: All compiled in-water explosions, including the eight WW2 events, plot well below the Murphy line; the authors propose the same slope offset by one magnitude unit for in-water sources.
disagreements.quote: As expected, all in-water explosions fall well below the standard Murphy (20) relationship which was derived from [...] .

disagreements.target: Gitterman and Shapira (2001) Dead Sea yield-magnitude relationship
disagreements.support: By visual comparison in Fig. 6, the modified Murphy line accounts for the compiled data better; the Dead Sea relation is attributed to the high water density of that specific environment.
disagreements.quote: it does account better than the Gitterman (2001) relationship, which has a different slope
